name: Ivan Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead vehicle-inspection booking software at a small tech company, where I am among the strongest developers. I use AI every day to draft tests but verify them with garage rosters. Asa, my partner, runs a cafe, our children are grown, and lower lead pay, rent and a recent cafe refrigerator repair leave us about two weeks saved with few similar local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our vehicle-inspection booking team that a little AI help is useful for finding a duplicate appointment, but a car still needs a real slot and inspector. I use AI every day to draft code tests and check them against the garage calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this small tech-company team; I am good at finding why a booking broke. The firm pays below the usual lead rate, and Asa’s cafe needed a new refrigerator, so rent and equipment bills have left us about two weeks of expenses saved; our children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the booking code and one missed-appointment report each Monday. We would bring lunches from home and save 30 monthly only if both incomes and cafe repairs allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about money even with little AI change. A broken cafe fridge can eat the week’s wages before the software has a single fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What booking went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage had one inspection bay but two cars were given the same slot. I matched the calendar to the inspector roster before either driver arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me draft unusual booking cases quickly. I still run the test and ask the garage to confirm the bay before releasing a change.

I use **AI daily** to draft tests, then verify them.
think: I have **two weeks saved** despite senior skill because cafe repairs and low local pay consumed cash.
I worry about **cafe repair bills** leaving too little for our rented home.
do: **Review booking code** and Monday missed-appointment reports.
**Bring lunches from home**; save 30 only if both incomes and cafe repairs allow.
S0.quote: A broken cafe fridge can eat the week’s wages before the software has a single fault.
fieldNote: His **lead ability** coexist with low pay at a small local firm.
The **cafe equipment bill** explains the thin cushion despite two sources of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, checking and coding could handle most routine garage appointments. I would keep a named inspector responsible for the final safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one engineer checks generated schedules for several garages. Two weeks saved and few nearby software jobs make a pay cut dangerous, even if I can use AI well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to pilot a new AI inspection-slot checker on fake garages, with an inspector reviewing each conflict. If approved, I’d test one doubled bay weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local vehicle-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and cafe bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and eager to test the checker. A booking can be clever and still put two cars in one bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would see the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garage inspector would compare the two fake appointments with the real bay rules. I would not let the pilot change a live schedule without sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the cafe money for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Asa needs it for stock and repairs; the company must fund paid testing of a work tool.

say: I want **inspector sign-off** before automated booking changes reach a live garage.
I want **fake garages** used for a paid trial before any live appointment is touched.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** despite daily AI use.
I cannot absorb **rent and cafe bills** from two weeks saved.
do: **Pilot AI slot checker** weekly only with approved paid time, fake garages and inspector sign-off.
**Search paid vehicle-software work** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and cafe bills.
S1.quote: A booking can be clever and still put two cars in one bay.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** goes beyond existing daily test drafting and requires paid approval.
The **cafe bills** raise the wage floor for any local replacement job.

steps.text: Pilot AI inspection-slot checker weekly on fake garages only with paid approval and inspector sign-off
Search paid local vehicle-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and cafe bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write booking code and assess inspection records cheaper than our team. Robots doing physical car inspections and cafe work may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer job could end, despite being good at it. Two weeks saved and Asa’s uneven cafe income would not keep rent and stock paid while I searched for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop buying lunches out and ask for written notice of any lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local garage-booking desk vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and cafe bills; I would ask the public employment office what help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage that keeps the cafe and flat steady. A full inspection calendar is not a full household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would garage desk work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know; AGI may do that too. I would take only an actual paid opening, not call it a protected career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children put money into the cafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not ask them to shore up our plan. They have their own households, and we need to manage the cafe from its own earnings.

I expect **inspection robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end.
I cannot carry **rent and cafe stock** on two weeks saved.
do: **Stop bought lunches** and request written lead-cut notice now.
**Apply for garage-desk vacancies** after 2028 loss only if paid local openings cover rent and cafe bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Alarmed** about lost wage and household bills.
S2.quote: A full inspection calendar is not a full household budget.
fieldNote: His **garage-desk option** may also be automated and needs a real paid vacancy.
He checks **public eligibility** rather than assuming a benefit will fund the cafe.

steps.text: Stop buying work lunches when lead developer cuts threaten
Apply for local paid garage-desk vacancies after 2028 loss if wages cover rent and cafe bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to learn the physical inspection rules before the software changes. Robots inspecting cars may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how an inspector decides whether a car is roadworthy, but my code skill does not qualify me to inspect a vehicle. Our cafe and rent leave no money for unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a local garage and my employer about a paid supervised inspection trainee vacancy. If a real place covers rent and cafe bills, funds the safety certificate and my employer approves paid time, I’d enrol and practise checking lights and brakes with a qualified inspector; we would save 35 monthly only while both incomes and cafe costs allow, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local inspection roles only if qualified and wages cover rent and cafe bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code job but glad to test a practical path. A safety stamp must come from a trained eye, not my keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspector check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspector would repeat my light and brake measurements and show me the rule I missed. I would not sign a roadworthiness report alone as a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no paid place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer wage and the cafe reserve intact. I would not call a garage visit a completed apprenticeship.

say: I want **supervised inspection training** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **inspection robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I need **current safety training** before any inspection role.
I cannot afford **unpaid trainee months** with cafe bills.
do: **Enrol in inspection training** only with paid vacancy covering rent and cafe, funded certificate, employer-approved time and qualified supervision.
**Save 35 monthly** only while both incomes and cafe costs allow.

feel: **Anxious but practical** about a funded trainee route.

The **cafe costs** remain part of the wage floor while training or seeking another job.

Save 35 monthly only while both incomes and cafe costs allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives us time to learn vehicle rules and rebuild the cafe reserve. Robots inspecting cars and working in cafes may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need a wage at 68 and have not checked a retirement amount. The two weeks saved today worry me more than a distant title for my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing booking code and save 40 monthly only while both incomes and cafe repairs allow. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local garage operations vacancies only if I qualify and wages cover rent and cafe bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about our present bills despite the decade. A longer calendar does not put cash into the till today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for a garage job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would look among local garages and software firms first. Asa’s cafe lease and customers are here, so I am not making a move plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children cover the cafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own rent and work, and I will not use their pay in our household plan.

I need **current developer pay** for rent and cafe costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end while cafe and rent bills continue. Written notice, a real paid garage vacancy covering both and verified temporary public help would give us a route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a good booking system can keep our cafe open without my wage. A booking system cannot pay our cafe’s fridge bill without my wage.

headlineQuote: A booking system cannot pay our cafe’s fridge bill without my wage.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, low pay and two weeks saved.
He and Asa **rent** while her cafe faces stock and repair costs; grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but checks bookings against garage rosters.
He considers **paid inspection training** only with funded certification, supervision and wages covering rent and cafe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before a paid local garage role exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a rent-and-cafe-covering local vacancy and verified public help would matter.
